5202:
Months began with the new moon, giving a year of about 354 days; to keep festivals tied to the harvests an extra month (a second Adar) was added roughly seven times in nineteen years. Pre-exilic texts use Canaanite month names such as Abib, Ziv, Ethanim and Bul (Exod 13:4; 1 Kgs 6:1; 1 Kgs 6:38; 1 Kgs 8:2), while post-exilic books use Babylonian names: Nisan, Iyyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Av, Elul, Tishri, Marcheshvan, Kislev, Tevet, Shevat and Adar (Neh 2:1; Esth 3:7). The religious year began in spring with Nisan (Exod 12:2), while the civil and agricultural year turned in autumn. The Qumran community and the book of Jubilees championed a rival 364-day solar calendar, so not all Jews kept feasts on the same days.

The Torah required men to appear before the LORD three times a year (Exod 23:14-17; Deut 16:16). Passover on 14 Nisan, followed by the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread, recalled the exodus and coincided with the barley harvest (Exod 12:1-20; Lev 23:4-14). The Feast of Weeks, fifty days later and so called Pentecost in Greek, celebrated the wheat harvest (Lev 23:15-21; Acts 2:1). The Feast of Booths or Tabernacles, from 15 Tishri, marked the fruit and olive ingathering, with families living in shelters to recall the wilderness (Lev 23:33-43). In the first century water was drawn from Siloam and poured at the altar and great lamps lit the temple courts, the background to Jesus' words about living water and the light of the world (John 7:37-38; John 8:12).

Autumn also brought the day of trumpets on 1 Tishri (Lev 23:23-25), later Rosh Hashanah, and the Day of Atonement on 10 Tishri, a fast day of national cleansing (Lev 16:29-34; Lev 23:26-32); Luke dates a dangerous voyage by it, calling it 'the Fast' (Acts 27:9). Later feasts were Purim in Adar, commemorating deliverance in Esther's day (Esth 9:20-32), and Hanukkah or Dedication in Kislev, commemorating the Maccabean rededication of the temple, at which Jesus was in Jerusalem (John 10:22-23).

Pilgrim crowds swelled Jerusalem at Passover. Josephus gives figures in the millions that are generally thought inflated; modern estimates range from around a hundred thousand to several hundred thousand. John's gospel structures Jesus' ministry around at least three Passovers (John 2:13; John 6:4; John 11:55). Whether the Last Supper was itself a Passover meal, as the Synoptics present it (Mark 14:12-16), or held the evening before, with Jesus dying as the lambs were slaughtered, as John's timing may suggest (John 18:28; John 19:14), is an old and unresolved question.
5206: Fifty days after Passover (May/June), wheat harvest
5209: 15-21 Tishri, plus an eighth day of assembly
5215: From Tiglath-pileser III onward, Assyria systematically moved conquered populations across its empire to break resistance and supply labor. This policy ended the northern kingdom of Israel and created the mixed population of Samaria.
5216:
Mass deportation was an Assyrian imperial tool before the eighth century, but Tiglath-pileser III (745-727 BC) made it routine and two-directional: rebels were removed from their homeland and replaced by peoples from elsewhere. The aims were practical: to break local loyalties, punish revolt, populate new cities and farmland, and supply soldiers and workers. Assyriologist Bustenay Oded estimated that some four and a half million people were moved over about three centuries, though such totals are necessarily rough. Assyrian reliefs show deportees walking with their families and belongings, not chained in long lines, because they were valuable as settlers.

Israel felt this in stages. Tiglath-pileser took Galilee, Gilead and the territory of Naphtali in 733/732 BC and carried the people to Assyria (2 Kgs 15:29). After a three-year siege Samaria fell in 722/721 BC; Shalmaneser V began the siege and Sargon II claims the conquest, recording in his inscriptions that he deported 27,290 people (other copies give 27,280). The biblical account places the exiles in Halah, on the Habor river of Gozan and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17:5-6), and says the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim to resettle Samaria (2 Kgs 17:24). The narrator explains the disaster theologically as the result of covenant unfaithfulness (2 Kgs 17:7-23), as Hosea and Amos had warned (Hos 9:3; Amos 7:17).

Judah nearly suffered the same fate. In 701 BC Sennacherib took Lachish and many towns; his prism claims he took 200,150 people from Judah, a figure many think inflated, and his Nineveh palace reliefs show Lachish's families being led away. His envoy offered Jerusalem's defenders peaceful deportation 'to a land like your own land' (2 Kgs 18:31-32), but the city was spared (2 Kgs 19:32-36; Isa 37:33-37).

The resettlement of Samaria lies behind later Jewish-Samaritan hostility, since Judeans described the Samaritans as descendants of these colonists (2 Kgs 17:24-41). The idea of 'ten lost tribes' is too simple: many northerners stayed or fled south, Hezekiah invited survivors to Passover (2 Chr 30:1-11), and Luke introduces Anna as from the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36). Assyria's brutality explains why Jonah resisted preaching to Nineveh and why Nahum celebrates its fall in 612 BC (Jonah 4:1-2; Nah 3:1-7).
5218: Reigned 745-727 BC; made two-way deportation standard policy
5224: 200,150 people taken from Judah in 701 BC (likely inflated)
5226: From Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, Sepharvaim (2 Kgs 17:24)
5228: Judeans were taken to Babylonia in several waves between 605 and 582 BC, where they mostly lived in their own communities as farmers and workers. Exile reshaped Judaism around scripture, Sabbath and identity without a temple.
5229:
Babylon took captives from Judah in stages. Daniel and other young nobles were taken around 605 BC (Dan 1:1-6). In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar deported King Jehoiachin, his court, warriors and craftsmen, about ten thousand people including Ezekiel (2 Kgs 24:10-16). After the rebellion of Zedekiah, Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed in 586 BC and more were taken (2 Kgs 25:8-12), and a further deportation followed in 582 BC; Jeremiah gives totals of 3,023, 832 and 745, 4,600 in all, probably counting adult men (Jer 52:28-30). The poorest were left to work the land (2 Kgs 25:12).

Unlike the Assyrians, the Babylonians did not usually import foreigners into conquered land, and they settled deportees in groups. Ezekiel lived among exiles at Tel-abib by the Chebar canal near Nippur (Ezek 1:1-3; Ezek 3:15), and elders could gather in his house (Ezek 8:1). Cuneiform tablets from a town called Al-Yahudu, 'Judah-town', dating from about 572 to 477 BC, show Judeans farming land held from the crown, paying taxes, making contracts and giving children names built on the divine name Yahweh. Ration tablets found in Babylon list oil for 'Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahud', confirming Jehoiachin's presence at court and his later release (2 Kgs 25:27-30).

Jeremiah's letter told the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, marry and seek the welfare of the city, because the exile would last seventy years (Jer 29:4-10). Some rose high in the administration, as Daniel and his friends did, receiving Babylonian names and education while trying to keep their distinct practices (Dan 1:4-8). Others mourned bitterly by the rivers of Babylon (Ps 137:1-6).

Without the temple, identity centered on what could be carried: circumcision, Sabbath, food laws, prayer toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10), and above all the scriptures, which many scholars think were collected and edited in this period. Prophets such as Ezekiel and the later chapters of Isaiah reinterpreted the catastrophe as judgment and promised a new exodus (Ezek 36:24-28; Isa 40:1-5). When Cyrus allowed return, many stayed; Babylonian Jewry remained a major center for more than a thousand years and later produced the Babylonian Talmud.
5240: c. 572-477 BC, records of a Judean village in Babylonia
5241: Persian Policy and the Cyrus Cylinder
5242: Cyrus the Great took Babylon in 539 BC and, like later Persian kings, allowed deported peoples and their gods to return home. The Cyrus Cylinder records this policy, and Ezra-Nehemiah describe its effect on Judah.
5243:
Cyrus II of Persia captured Babylon in October 539 BC, largely without a battle. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay barrel inscribed in Akkadian and discovered at Babylon in 1879, presents him as chosen by Babylon's god Marduk to replace the impious Nabonidus. It says he returned the images of gods to their sanctuaries in cities across the Tigris and gathered their former inhabitants back to their homes. The cylinder does not mention Judah, and the policy was conventional royal propaganda as well as pragmatic statecraft: restored local cults prayed for the king and kept provinces content. Even so, it matches the biblical picture well.

The Bible records Cyrus' decree in Hebrew (Ezra 1:1-4; 2 Chr 36:22-23) and in an Aramaic memorandum found later in the archive at Ecbatana, which specifies the temple's dimensions and that costs be paid from the royal treasury (Ezra 6:1-5). Isaiah names Cyrus as the LORD's shepherd and anointed (Isa 44:28-45:1); traditional scholars see predictive prophecy, while many critical scholars date these chapters to the exile itself, a question bound up with views of inspiration. The returning exiles, led by Sheshbazzar and then Zerubbabel and Joshua, numbered 42,360 plus servants (Ezra 2:64-65).

The Persian empire was organized into satrapies with Imperial Aramaic as the administrative language, which is why parts of Ezra are in Aramaic (Ezra 4:8-6:18; Ezra 7:12-26). Opposition from neighbors delayed the temple until Darius I confirmed Cyrus' decree; it was finished in 515 BC (Ezra 6:6-15). Artaxerxes I sent Ezra the scribe with authority to teach and enforce the law of God (Ezra 7:11-26) and later appointed his cupbearer Nehemiah governor to rebuild Jerusalem's walls (Neh 2:1-8). A royal courier system carried edicts quickly across the empire, as Esther describes (Esth 3:13-15; Esth 8:10).

Papyri from Elephantine, a Jewish military colony on the Nile, illuminate the period: a letter of 407 BC asks Bagohi, governor of Judah, for permission to rebuild their destroyed temple of Yahu, and mentions Sanballat's sons in Samaria (compare Neh 2:19). Persian rule over Judea lasted about two centuries, until Alexander's conquest in 332 BC, and Daniel and Esther both portray Jews serving at the Persian court (Dan 6:1-3; Esth 2:5-8).
5247: Akkadian clay cylinder found at Babylon in 1879; now in the British Museum
5254: After Alexander the Great's conquests, Greek language, cities and culture spread across the Near East, including Judea. Jews adopted, adapted and resisted Hellenism in varying degrees, and the New Testament itself was written in Greek.
5255:
Alexander of Macedon defeated Persia at Issus in 333 BC, besieged Tyre and Gaza in 332, and took control of Judea on the way to Egypt. After his death in 323 BC his generals divided the empire. Judea was ruled by the Ptolemies of Egypt until about 200 BC, when the Seleucids of Syria won it at the battle of Panium. Daniel's visions of the goat with a great horn broken into four and of the kings of the north and south are commonly read against this history (Dan 8:5-8; Dan 8:21-22; Dan 11:2-4).

Hellenization meant Greek as the common language of trade and government (*koine*, 'common' Greek), Greek-style cities with gymnasium, theater and council, and Greek education, philosophy and religion. In Alexandria, Jews translated their scriptures into Greek from the third century BC; the legend in the *Letter of Aristeas* attributes the Torah's translation to seventy-two elders, hence the name Septuagint. In Jerusalem the high priest Jason built a gymnasium around 175 BC, and some young men tried to hide their circumcision (1 Maccabees 1:14-15; 2 Maccabees 4:9-15), provoking deep division.

By the first century Greek cities ringed Galilee: the Decapolis east of the Jordan (Mark 5:20; Mark 7:31), coastal cities such as Caesarea, and Herodian foundations such as Sepphoris and Tiberias (John 6:23). Martin Hengel showed that Palestinian Judaism was itself thoroughly touched by Hellenism, so a sharp line between 'Palestinian' and 'Hellenistic' Judaism is misleading. Many Galileans were probably bilingual in Aramaic and some Greek, and Greek inscriptions and names are common even in Jerusalem.

The church was born into this world. Acts distinguishes Hebrew-speaking and Greek-speaking Jewish believers (Acts 6:1), and the seven chosen to serve all have Greek names (Acts 6:5). Greeks seek Jesus at the feast (John 12:20-21), Paul debates philosophers in Athens (Acts 17:16-34), and every New Testament book was written in Greek, usually quoting the Septuagint. How much Greek thought shaped early theology, for example John's use of *logos* (John 1:1), is debated.
5261: From the battle of Panium, c. 200 BC
5262: Greek Old Testament, begun in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC
5264: Built under the high priest Jason, c. 175 BC
5266: When Antiochus IV outlawed Judaism and defiled the temple in 167 BC, a priestly family led a revolt that rededicated the temple in 164 BC and founded the Hasmonean dynasty. Hanukkah commemorates the rededication.
5267:
Antiochus IV Epiphanes, Seleucid king from 175 BC, intervened repeatedly in Jerusalem's high-priestly politics and plundered the temple. Around 167 BC, after unrest in Jerusalem, he issued decrees banning circumcision, Sabbath observance and the Torah, and on 15 Kislev an altar to Olympian Zeus was set up on the altar of burnt offering, the 'abomination of desolation' (1 Maccabees 1:41-64). Daniel's visions describe a king who profanes the sanctuary, removes the regular burnt offering and sets up 'the abomination that makes desolate' (Dan 11:31; Dan 12:11), and Jesus later uses the phrase for a coming desecration (Matt 24:15; Mark 13:14).

At Modein the aged priest Mattathias killed a Jew offering pagan sacrifice and the king's officer, and fled to the hills with his five sons (1 Maccabees 2:15-28). His son Judas, nicknamed Maccabeus, 'the hammer', led guerrilla victories against larger Seleucid armies. On 25 Kislev 164 BC Judas' forces cleansed the temple, built a new altar and celebrated an eight-day dedication, decreeing that it be kept yearly (1 Maccabees 4:52-59). John's gospel places Jesus in the temple at this 'Feast of Dedication' in winter (John 10:22-23). The story of a single cruse of oil lasting eight days appears much later, in the Babylonian Talmud.

The revolt became a dynasty. Judas' brother Jonathan became high priest in 152 BC, and Simon won effective independence in 142 BC. John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea and forced its people to be circumcised, and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim. Alexander Jannaeus, king and high priest, was hated by the Pharisees and, according to Josephus, crucified eight hundred opponents (*Antiquities* 13.380). Civil war between his sons gave the Roman general Pompey the opportunity to take Jerusalem in 63 BC.

The Maccabean era shaped the world of the New Testament: it produced the parties of Pharisees and Sadducees, a tradition of zeal for the law, martyr stories that strengthened belief in bodily resurrection (2 Maccabees 7), and hopes for a liberator. Hebrews' list of those who were tortured, refusing release, to rise to a better life probably alludes to these martyrs (Heb 11:35-38). The books of Maccabees are in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles but in the Protestant Apocrypha.
5279: Rome controlled Judea from 63 BC, first through client kings and from AD 6 through governors such as Pontius Pilate. Roman power framed Jesus' trial, Paul's imprisonments and the catastrophe of AD 70.
5280:
Pompey entered Jerusalem in 63 BC and made Judea tributary. Rome then ruled through Hasmonean figures and, from 40/37 BC, through Herod the Great as client king. When Herod's son Archelaus proved incompetent, Augustus deposed him in AD 6 and placed Judea, with Samaria and Idumea, under an equestrian governor based at Caesarea Maritima, subordinate to the legate of Syria. Galilee remained under Herod Antipas, so Jesus grew up under a Jewish client ruler, while Jerusalem was under direct Roman rule. Luke dates events by the reigns of Augustus and Tiberius and the governorships of Quirinius and Pilate (Luke 2:1-2; Luke 3:1).

Pontius Pilate governed from AD 26 to 36; a stone found at Caesarea in 1961 names him 'prefect of Judea'. Governors commanded auxiliary troops, around three thousand, mostly recruited locally from non-Jewish cities, and moved to Jerusalem at festivals, garrisoning the Antonia fortress beside the temple, from which the tribune Claudius Lysias rescued Paul (Acts 21:31-36). Centurions appear often and sometimes sympathetically (Matt 8:5-13; Mark 15:39; Acts 10:1-2). Soldiers could compel civilians to carry loads, the background of 'going the second mile' and of Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross (Matt 5:41; Mark 15:21).

Rome usually left local matters to the high priest and council, but kept capital jurisdiction, as John notes (John 18:31). Jews were exempted from military service and from emperor sacrifice, offering sacrifices on the emperor's behalf instead. Tensions flared over taxes, images and money: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the census of AD 6 (Acts 5:37), Pilate provoked crowds with military standards and by taking temple funds for an aqueduct, and Luke mentions Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1). The question 'Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar?' was a trap precisely because of this (Mark 12:13-17).

After AD 44 governors such as Felix and Festus, before whom Paul appeared (Acts 24:1-27; Acts 25:1-12), presided over growing unrest. In AD 66 revolt broke out; Titus captured Jerusalem and burned the temple in August AD 70, and Masada fell in 73 or 74. Jesus' warnings about the temple's destruction (Mark 13:1-2; Luke 19:41-44; Luke 21:20-24) are read by some as fulfilled entirely in AD 70 and by others as foreshadowing a final end, a key question in eschatology. Paul's instruction to submit to governing authorities (Rom 13:1-7) and Revelation's portrait of Rome as a beast (Rev 13:1-8) show two sides of early Christian response.
5286: Prefect AD 26-36; named on the Pilate Stone at Caesarea
5288: A Roman mile was about 1,480 m (Matt 5:41)
5292: Herod the Great and his descendants ruled parts of the Jewish homeland as Roman clients from 37 BC to the end of the first century. Five different Herods appear in the New Testament, and keeping them apart clarifies many passages.
5293:
Herod the Great was the son of Antipater, an Idumean whose family had been converted under the Hasmoneans. Rome's Senate named him king of Judea in 40 BC, and he took Jerusalem in 37 BC. He was a gifted administrator and one of antiquity's great builders: he rebuilt the temple on a vast platform, created the artificial harbor city of Caesarea Maritima, and built palace-fortresses at Masada, Machaerus and the Herodium, where archaeologist Ehud Netzer identified his tomb in 2007. He was also paranoid and brutal, executing his wife Mariamne and three of his sons. Matthew's account of the massacre of Bethlehem's infants (Matt 2:1-18) is not attested elsewhere but fits his character. He died in 4 BC on the usual reckoning, which is why Jesus' birth is dated before then; a minority argue for 1 BC.

Herod's will divided his realm among three sons, confirmed by Augustus. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea as ethnarch, and his reputation is why Joseph settled in Galilee rather than Judea (Matt 2:22-23); he was deposed in AD 6. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch until AD 39, built Tiberias, married his half-brother's wife Herodias, imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist (Mark 6:14-29), was called 'that fox' by Jesus (Luke 13:31-32) and questioned Jesus during his trial (Luke 23:6-12). Philip ruled the north-east, refounding Paneas as Caesarea Philippi and Bethsaida as Julias (Luke 3:1; Mark 8:27).

Herod Agrippa I, a grandson of Herod the Great raised in Rome, became king over nearly all his grandfather's territory by AD 41. He executed James the son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter, and died suddenly at Caesarea in AD 44 after accepting divine acclaim (Acts 12:1-23); Josephus describes the same death (*Antiquities* 19.343-350). His son Agrippa II, with his sister Bernice, heard Paul's defense before Festus and remarked that Paul would soon persuade him to be a Christian (Acts 25:13-26:32). Agrippa I's daughter Drusilla was the wife of the governor Felix (Acts 24:24).

The 'Herodians' who joined Pharisees against Jesus were probably supporters of the dynasty (Mark 3:6; Mark 12:13). For many Jews the Herods were compromised: Idumean in origin, Roman in loyalty and Hellenistic in style, yet patrons of the temple. Their story frames the New Testament from Jesus' birth to Paul's last hearing in Judea.
5295: King 37-4 BC (named king by Rome 40 BC)
5297: Ethnarch of Judea, Samaria, Idumea, 4 BC-AD 6 (Matt 2:22)
5299: Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, 4 BC-AD 39

5307: First-century Jews owed Roman tribute, tolls and customs, Herodian taxes, and religious dues such as tithes and the temple tax. Toll collectors, who worked for these systems and often profited from them, were widely despised.
